archetype.name: Pocket Passer (intermediate attacker)
archetype.definition: A tall, rhythm-based thrower who now wins mostly from the pocket by driving the ball into the 10-to-19-yard window, with his legs a minor part of the plan this year.

report.headline: Lawrence's accuracy leap is real; the touchdown rate and deep-ball efficiency will cool.
report.take:
Lawrence has spent five seasons as a high-volume starter whose accuracy never matched his reputation. His completion rate over expected sat below zero in three of the last four years, and last season it was -1.9 even as the team went 13-4. Six games into 2026, the profile has flipped. His CPOE is 5.55 (8th of 45), his EPA per dropback is 0.275 (8th), and his bad-throw rate has dropped to 10.3%, 5th-best among charted passers and below every season on his record. The ball is also coming out faster, 2.72 seconds to throw against 2.87 a year ago. This is not a dink-and-dunk renaissance. His aggressiveness and intended air yards look like last year's. He is simply hitting the throws he used to miss.

The engine is the intermediate game. On 53 throws between 10 and 19 air yards he has added 0.623 EPA per attempt with a 64.2% success rate, and throws of 10-plus air yards account for 51.9 of his 54 dropback EPA. Under 10 yards he is merely fine at 0.162 per play. The middle of the field is where it pays most (0.675 per attempt). Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers are the beneficiaries, both well above 0.4 EPA per target. Brian Thomas Jr. sits at 0.088 on 20 targets, which says the offense is running through the slot and the seams rather than the outside vertical game.

What the numbers flatter: a 7.6% touchdown rate (5th) that puts him on a 40-touchdown pace, built partly on 9 red-zone scores despite a 51.4% completion rate there. On top of that, 20 deep attempts are producing 0.943 EPA per throw on a 45% completion rate. Both are small, hot samples well above anything in his career, and both will cool. What they hide: interceptions remain his tax. His 2.2% INT rate is only league average and ranks 30th, three of his four picks came on third down, and his late-and-close play (30 snaps, 0.082 EPA, -7 CPOE) has been his weakest situation. The two fumbles he hasn't lost are luck, not skill.

The recent path is quieter than the season line suggests, in both directions. The opening blowout of Cleveland (19 EPA) props up the averages, and his last five games sit at 0.202 EPA per dropback. But the last three have climbed back to 0.283 with more volume, 288 yards a game. The one soft spot is accuracy: his CPOE has slipped to 1.4 over that stretch, with negative marks in each of the last two games as attempts rose toward 40. Now he loses his starting right tackle, Anton Harrison, for the year. Expect a good, not historic, passer from here: still well above average, with fewer touchdowns per throw.

strengths.title: Intermediate throws carry the offense
strengths.body: His 10-to-19-yard throws are the most productive part of his game, with high success and a 7.1 CPOE, and they produce most of his passing value. He has a large enough sample (53 attempts) to trust the skill. The per-play rate will likely ease from 0.623, but this is a repeatable strength built on timing with Washington and Meyers over the middle.

strengths.title: Accuracy jump with real support
strengths.body: A 7.4-point CPOE gain on last season looks like a blip at first glance. But his bad-throw rate has fallen by 3.6 points to a career best, and he is getting the ball out faster. The charting backs the result, so a good part of this should hold, even if the full 5.55 CPOE drifts back toward his 2022 level.

strengths.title: Efficient sack avoidance
strengths.body: A 5.2% sack rate sits well under the league's 6.7%. His 24.4% pressure-to-sack rate is mid-pack, better than the 29-30% marks of 2023 and 2025. Quicker processing is the likely cause, and that matters now that the line is weaker.

concerns.title: Interceptions never went away
concerns.body: His INT rate ranks 30th of 45, and turnovers have been a career-long issue, with 12 or more picks in three seasons. The damage clusters on third down (3 of his 4 picks, at an average of 9 yards to go), where he forces throws on long distances. This is a trait, not noise. Expect roughly one pick every game or two.

concerns.title: Touchdown and deep rates will regress
concerns.body: A 7.6% TD rate is far above anything in his career. The red-zone and deep-ball numbers driving it come from small samples: 35 red-zone attempts at 51.4% completion and 20 deep throws at 0.943 EPA apiece. Over the rest of the season both numbers should come down meaningfully, even if the overall efficiency holds.

concerns.title: Right tackle loss and fading accuracy
concerns.body: Anton Harrison, a 92%-snap starter, tore his ACL and is on injured reserve. That arrives just as Lawrence's CPOE has dipped in heavier-volume games, and his close fourth-quarter play is already his weakest situation. More pressure off the right side would test the quicker release that has kept his sacks down.

trend.note: After a dominant opener and a flat loss at Denver, his efficiency has held near 0.28 EPA per dropback over the last three games while volume rose toward 300 yards a game, though his CPOE has turned negative in the two most recent games.

nextGame.headline: Rested Lawrence gets a thin Colts secondary at home
nextGame.body:
Indianapolis is a middling pass defense (18th in pass EPA allowed) that guards the deep ball well but gives up efficiency underneath. It ranks 10th in deep EPA allowed and 22nd on short throws, and its 26th-ranked hit rate means it rarely gets home. That fits Lawrence's current game: quick, timing-based throws into the short and intermediate areas rather than living on shots. The Colts offense is 30th in pass EPA and without tight end Tyler Warren. That is why Jacksonville is a 7.5-point home favorite, and it raises the chance of a lead that leans the second half toward the run.

Availability tilts his way. Sauce Gardner, an 89%-snap corner, is out and Justin Walley is questionable with a knee injury, thinning the coverage that has held opposing WR2s down. Against that, this is Lawrence's first game without right tackle Anton Harrison, though a weak Colts rush is a soft landing for his replacement. He comes off the bye on 14 days' rest. The forecast, still days out, shows a thunderstorm chance with modest wind. Worth monitoring, not a reason to downgrade yet.

keyMatchups.title: Underneath game versus soft middle
keyMatchups.body: The Colts allow positive EPA on short throws and are tougher deep, which steers Lawrence toward his strength in the 0-19 yard range. Expect Washington and Meyers working the middle rather than many vertical shots.

keyMatchups.title: Third receiver role is exposed
keyMatchups.body: Indianapolis has been torched by WR3s at 0.77 EPA per target, 31st in the league, while smothering WR2s. If Brian Thomas Jr. holds the third receiver role, this is a spot for his quiet 0.088 EPA per target to turn, especially with Gardner out.

keyMatchups.title: Blowout script caps volume
keyMatchups.body: With the Colts offense struggling, a multi-score lead is plausible. He has been efficient when leading big (0.53 EPA per play), but those situations bring fewer attempts and more handoffs.

nextGame.watch: How the right side holds up without Harrison on obvious passing downs, where Lawrence's third-down interceptions have come.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy gain is supported by charting (fewer bad throws, faster release), so a well-above-average efficiency level should hold. The touchdown rate, the deep-ball returns and the red-zone scoring are the parts running hot. Expect touchdowns closer to 1.6-2.2 per game than his current pace, with yardage steady around 230-275 as the offense keeps leaning on his arm in an otherwise balanced attack.

Interceptions should stay a steady, modest drain, in line with his whole career, and his rushing is a minor add at roughly 8-18 yards a game, well below his usual seasons. The biggest unknown is the line: losing Harrison could push his pressure and sack numbers back toward 2023-2025 levels, which would test whether the quicker processing is real.
swingFactors: Whether the CPOE gain holds as volume rises

confidence.note: Six games of strong efficiency backed by charting, but touchdown and deep samples are small and the line just lost a starter.
